content: Dysuria refers to the experience of pain, discomfort, or a burning sensation during urination. This pain may be localized to the area where urine exits the body, or it may be felt deeper within, such as behind the pubic bone, in the bladder, or in the prostate. Dysuria is a relatively common condition, and individuals experiencing it may also feel an increased urge to urinate. The most common causes of dysuria include infections or inflammation within the urinary tract. In men, urethritis caused by sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhea or chlamydia is a frequent cause. In women and girls, dysuria may result from several factors, including changes in vaginal tissue due to menopause (atrophic vaginitis), genital herpes infections, irritation from products like bubble baths, perfumes, or lotions, or infections of the vulva and vagina (vulvovaginitis), such as yeast infections. Other potential causes include interstitial cystitis, prostate infections (prostatitis), and damage to the bladder lining from radiation therapy (radiation cystitis). Certain individuals are at higher risk of developing dysuria. These include people with multiple sexual partners or those who engage in sexual activity with an infected partner. It is important to seek medical attention promptly if you experience any of the following: discharge from the penis or vagina, painful urination lasting more than one day, blood in the urine, fever, or if you are pregnant and experiencing painful urination. To diagnose dysuria, a healthcare provider will conduct a physical examination and ask detailed questions about your symptoms and medical history. These questions may include inquiries about the onset and duration of the pain, whether it occurs exclusively during urination, the presence of other symptoms such as back pain, fever, or abnormal urine odor, and any recent changes in urination patterns. Diagnostic tests such as urinalysis and urine culture may be performed. In women with vaginal discharge, a pelvic exam and analysis of vaginal fluids may be necessary. Men with penile discharge may require a urethral swab. Treatment for dysuria depends on the underlying cause. For example, infections may require antibiotics, while other causes may necessitate different interventions. The prognosis for dysuria varies depending on its cause. However, complications can arise if the condition is not treated, including cystitis, pyelonephritis, or urinary tract infections. To flush bacteria from the bladder, it is recommended to drink several glasses of water daily. Women should wipe from front to back after bowel movements and urinate after sexual intercourse. To prevent irritation-related dysuria, women should keep the genital area clean and dry, change tampons and sanitary napkins frequently, and avoid using irritating products such as soaps, vaginal sprays, and douches. Female children should limit bubble baths and be gently but thoroughly cleaned after playing in sand or wearing wet swimsuits for extended periods, as these can cause vulvar irritation (vulvitis). To prevent dysuria caused by sexually transmitted infections, individuals should either abstain from sex or maintain a monogamous relationship with an uninfected partner. If there is a risk of infection, latex condoms should be used during sexual activity.
